t: Minimum Absolute Difference Queries — Prefix Presence Counts Over a 100-Value Domain
o: For each query [l, r] we need the smallest gap between two DIFFERENT values inside the slice; slices whose elements are all equal yield -1. Example 1 (nums = [1,3,4,8]): the four queries produce [2, 1, 4, 1], where [0,3]'s answer comes from |3-4| = 1 even though 8 is present. Example 2 shows both regimes: query [2,3] sees only [2,2] and answers -1, while [3,5] over [2,7,10] answers |7-10| = 3. Sorting every slice independently costs up to O(n log n) per query — hopeless for many queries. The lever is the value domain: nums[i] <= 100, so each query can afford a scan over values 1..100 as long as presence-in-range is answerable quickly per value, which prefix occurrence counts (or sorted position lists) provide.
k: The minimum absolute difference over distinct values equals the minimum gap between CONSECUTIVE distinct values in sorted order.
Values lie in 1..100, so a query reduces to knowing WHICH values occur in [l, r]; scanning at most 100 candidates finishes each query.
Prefix counts cnt[i][v] = occurrences of v among the first i elements give presence-in-range in O(1); storing sorted position lists per value plus binary search works too.

a.i: Extract the slice, deduplicate, sort, and take the minimum difference of adjacent distinct representatives. This directly mirrors the definition and is trivially correct, but per-query cost grows with slice length, which is fatal for long ranges.
s: Collect nums[l..r] into a set and sort its distinct values.
If fewer than two distinct values exist, append -1.
Otherwise append the minimum difference between consecutive sorted values.
a.t: O(q x n log n) worst case — each query sorts its own slice of up to n elements.
a.sp: O(n) — temporary storage for the largest slice.

a.i: Preprocess once: either full prefix counts per value or, more compactly, a sorted list of positions for each value 1..100. Per query, sweep v from 1 to 100; v occurs in [l, r] iff prefix[r+1][v] - prefix[l][v] > 0 (or the first position >= l in pos[v] is <= r). Track the previously seen occurring value so consecutive occurring values update the best gap; fewer than two occurring values means -1. Each query costs one pass over the 100-value domain.
s: Precompute presence data: prefix count tables per value (C++/Java) or per-value sorted position lists (Python/JavaScript).
Per query [l, r]: initialize prevSeen = -1 and best = infinity.
For v = 1..100: test whether v occurs in [l, r].
When it occurs: if prevSeen != -1, best = min(best, v - prevSeen); then set prevSeen = v.
Append best, or -1 when best stayed infinite.
a.t: O(n + q x 100 log n) with position lists (O(1) presence tests instead with prefix-count tables) — linear preprocessing plus a bounded domain scan per query.
a.sp: O(n) for per-value position lists (O(100 x n) for full prefix-count tables).

w: Spot the tiny value domain immediately — it converts a range-minimization problem into a counting problem, exactly like other frequency-range classics. Pitfalls: returning 0 when duplicates exist (equal pairs are disallowed by definition — compare only DISTINCT values), forgetting the -1 for uniform slices, and sorting slices per query. State the consecutive-distinct-values fact explicitly; it justifies comparing adjacent occurring values in the sweep. Follow-up: values up to 10^9 (coordinate-compress first), dynamic point updates (a segment tree storing per-node value counts), or maximizing instead of minimizing the gap.
